message.content:
No, not under the usual definition of finite expectation.
Let X and Y be discrete random variables.
Assume E(X) is finite.
Assume E(Y) is finite.
Then both variables are integrable.
That means E|X| is finite.
That also means E|Y| is finite.
The triangle inequality applies to absolute values.
We have |X + Y| <= |X| + |Y|.
Therefore E|X + Y| is finite.
Thus X + Y is integrable.
Its expectation exists and is finite.
Linearity of expectation gives the result.
We get E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).
The right side is finite because both terms are finite.
So the sum expectation cannot be undefined.
It also cannot be infinite.
This conclusion uses discrete variables.
It also holds for general random variables.
The only way failure can occur is if an expectation is not integrable.
For example, positive and negative parts may both be infinite.
Then the expectation is undefined rather than finite.
The final answer is that no such discrete random variable pair exists because finite expectations for both variables in every case now guarantee integrability and linearity then keeps the sum expectation well defined beneath the conditions.
